The following description of embodiments refers to the accompanying drawings. The same reference numeral denotes the same part throughout. Terms of direction are used with respect to the frame of the clamp: the axis of the frame is the axis about which the frame is annular in the closed condition, "inward" and "radially inward" mean toward that axis, "outward" and "radially outward" mean away from it, and "circumferential" means about that axis. These terms describe relationships within the clamp and do not require the clamp to be used in any particular attitude.

Overall arrangement

FIG. 1 shows a split pipe clamp 100 in the closed condition around a pipe 90. The clamp 100 has a first frame half 10 and a second frame half 12. Each of the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 is semicircular, and the two frame halves together surround the pipe 90. The first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 are joined at one end, referred to as the hinge end, by a hinge 14, and are releasably joined at the other end, referred to as the latch end, by a releasable latch 16. The hinge 14 permits the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 to be swung apart far enough for the frame halves to be placed around the pipe 90 from the side. When the frame halves are brought together and the latch 16 is engaged, the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 define a frame that is annular about the axis of the clamp 100.

Three jaw carriages 30 are distributed around the frame in the closed condition, so that the three jaw carriages 30 approach the pipe 90 from three different directions. Each jaw carriage 30 moves radially with respect to the frame and carries at its inner end a jaw pad 40, which is described below in connection with FIG. 3. The jaw pads 40 carried at the inner ends of the three jaw carriages 30 bear on the pipe 90 when the clamp 100 is clamped. The clamp 100 does not require a part dimensioned to a particular pipe diameter, and the same clamp 100 serves pipes of different diameters within the radial travel of the jaw carriages 30.

The frame may carry a mounting boss 70 outside the annular guide 18 described below, as shown in FIG. 5, which is taken on a plane corresponding to the plane of FIG. 3. The mounting boss 70 supports a sensor, a tool, or a conduit that is to be held on the pipe 90 by the clamp 100. FIG. 5 shows equipment 80 supported on the mounting boss 70, the equipment 80 being a sensor, a tool, or a conduit. The mounting boss 70 does not participate in the advance of the three jaw carriages 30 inwardly in synchronism. Equipment carried at the mounting boss 70 therefore lies outside the drive path by which the jaws are advanced. The mounting boss 70 is an optional feature of the clamp 100 and may be omitted.

The segmented cam ring

FIG. 2 shows the segmented cam ring 20 of the clamp 100, drawn removed from the frame with its segments in the coupled condition. The segmented cam ring 20 comprises a first cam ring segment 22 and a second cam ring segment 24. The first cam ring segment 22 is carried by the first frame half 10 and the second cam ring segment 24 is carried by the second frame half 12, so that each frame half carries one segment of the ring and each segment travels with its own frame half when the clamp 100 is opened.

The first cam ring segment 22 and the second cam ring segment 24 meet at two places, one at the hinge end and one at the latch end. At the hinge end the two segments have complementary coupling faces 26, and at the latch end they have complementary coupling faces 28. The complementary coupling faces 26 and the complementary coupling faces 28 are circumferentially facing coupling faces, each pair being shaped so that one segment can transmit circumferential force to the other through the joint. The faces are brought into engagement by the same motion that closes the frame halves: as the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 are swung together about the hinge 14 and the latch 16 is engaged, the complementary coupling faces 26 close on one another at the hinge end and the complementary coupling faces 28 close on one another at the latch end.

Coupling the segments in this way solves a problem created by splitting the clamp. Here the division of the ring is undone by the act of closing the clamp. In the closed condition the first cam ring segment 22 and the second cam ring segment 24 are coupled at both ends and rotate together in the annular guide as a coupled ring, and a circumferential input applied to either segment is carried around the whole ring. One input, applied at one point on one frame half, therefore reaches every jaw carriage 30 through a single kinematic element, and the relationship between the jaw carriages 30 is set by the geometry of the ring rather than by the way the clamp is operated. When the latch 16 is released and the frame halves are swung apart, the complementary coupling faces 26 and the complementary coupling faces 28 separate and each segment stays with its own frame half, so that the coupling is made and broken by the closing and opening of the frame halves.

The segmented cam ring 20 has three oblique slots 34, one for each jaw carriage 30. Each oblique slot 34 is inclined to the radial direction of the frame at the circumferential position of that slot, so that rotation of the coupled ring produces inward travel of its jaw carriage 30, the three oblique slots 34 being arranged so that the three jaw carriages 30 travel inwardly in synchronism. The inclination of the oblique slots 34 sets the ratio between the circumferential stroke of the coupled ring and the radial travel of the jaw carriages 30.

The segmented cam ring 20 further has a ring drive face 36, shown in FIG. 2 at the latch end of the ring, against which the latch acts as described below. The ring drive face 36 is presented at a position on the ring that the wedge of the latch can reach, and it lies at an inclination to the direction in which that wedge advances, so that advance of the wedge moves the segmented cam ring 20 circumferentially.

The jaw carriages

FIG. 3 is a fragmentary sectional view through one jaw carriage 30, taken along line 3-3 of FIG. 1. The frame is channeled to form the annular guide 18, which receives the segmented cam ring 20. The annular guide 18 retains the first cam ring segment 22 on the first frame half 10 and the second cam ring segment 24 on the second frame half 12, and permits the coupled ring to move circumferentially.

The frame is further formed with a radial guide 38 at the position of each jaw carriage 30. Each jaw carriage 30 is received in a respective radial guide 38 and is constrained by the radial guide 38 to move radially with respect to the frame. Each jaw carriage 30 carries a follower 32 that projects from the jaw carriage 30 into a respective one of the oblique slots 34 of the segmented cam ring 20. The follower 32 bears against the sides of the oblique slot 34.

The follower 32 is constrained in two ways at once. The radial guide 38 prevents the jaw carriage 30, and therefore the follower 32, from moving circumferentially, while the oblique slot 34 holds the follower 32 at a position along the slot, which is inclined to the radial direction, so that circumferential movement of the segmented cam ring 20 displaces the follower 32 radially. When the coupled ring turns through its stroke, the side of each oblique slot 34 bears on the corresponding follower 32 and drives it, and with it the jaw carriage 30, radially inward along the radial guide 38. Because all three followers 32 are engaged in oblique slots 34 of one coupled ring, the three jaw carriages 30 advance inwardly in synchronism for as long as the ring turns. The jaw pads 40 therefore close on the pipe together.

At its inner end each jaw carriage 30 carries a jaw pad 40. The jaw pad 40 is pivotally mounted on the jaw carriage 30 and has a concave bearing face directed inwardly of the frame. Because the jaw pad 40 is free to pivot on the jaw carriage 30, the concave bearing face aligns itself with the outer surface of the pipe as it lands. The same concave bearing face therefore seats on pipes of different diameters, and no part dimensioned to a particular pipe diameter is required.

A carriage return spring 44 acts on each jaw carriage 30 so as to urge that jaw carriage 30 radially outward. When the latch 16 is released and the drive from the latch to the ring drive face 36 is removed, the carriage return springs 44 push the jaw carriages 30 outward and the jaw pads 40 are retracted from the pipe, and the clamp 100 is left with its jaw carriages 30 retracted and ready for the next installation. Retraction of the jaw carriages 30 clears the jaw pads 40 from the pipe before the frame halves are swung apart.

The latch and the force-limiting drive train

FIG. 4 is an enlarged fragmentary view of the latch end, with parts shown in section. The latch 16 includes a latch housing 58 at the latch end, a latch handle 50, a wedge 52, and a force-limiting spring stack 54 in the drive train between the latch handle 50 and the wedge 52. The latch housing 58 presents a fixed edge referred to below in connection with the indicator pin 56. The wedge 52 is positioned so that its inclined face bears on the ring drive face 36 of the segmented cam ring 20.

The latch 16 has two engaged positions. In a first position, the latch 16 holds the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 closed around the pipe 90 but does not clamp it: the frame is captive on the pipe 90 and cannot fall away, while the segmented cam ring 20 has not yet advanced the jaw carriages 30. In a second, over-center position, the wedge 52 drives the segmented cam ring 20 and the pipe 90 is clamped. Movement of the latch handle 50 from the first position to the second position advances the wedge 52 against the ring drive face 36. The inclined face of the wedge 52 converts that advance into circumferential movement of the segmented cam ring 20, and the coupled ring turns through its limited stroke.

The force-limiting spring stack 54 answers the problem of what becomes of the operator's remaining handle travel. The jaw pads 40 land on the pipe 90 at some point in the stroke that depends on the diameter of the pipe 90, and the latch handle 50 has still to be carried into its over-center position. If the drive train from the latch handle 50 to the wedge 52 were rigid, that remaining travel would be taken up by whatever part of the assembly yielded first, in practice by driving one jaw farther into the pipe 90 than the others and loading it far more heavily. Additional travel of the latch handle 50 after all three jaw pads 40 have contacted the pipe 90 compresses the force-limiting spring stack 54 rather than forcing one jaw carriage 30 farther inward than the others.

An indicator pin 56 is coupled to the force-limiting spring stack 54 and projects from the latch housing 58. As the force-limiting spring stack 54 compresses, the indicator pin 56 moves relative to a fixed edge of the latch housing 58, and the position of the indicator pin 56 with respect to that fixed edge shows the operator when the force-limiting spring stack 54 has entered a predetermined compression range. The indicator pin 56 therefore reports clamp loading mechanically, and what it reports is the state of the force-limiting spring stack 54. It is not a measurement of the diameter of the pipe 90.

Operation

To install the clamp 100 on a pipe 90, the operator opens the latch 16 and swings the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 apart about the hinge 14. The first cam ring segment 22 stays with the first frame half 10 and the second cam ring segment 24 stays with the second frame half 12, and the complementary coupling faces 26 and the complementary coupling faces 28 are separated. The operator places the frame halves around the pipe 90 from the side and closes them about the hinge 14. Closing the frame halves brings the complementary coupling faces 26 into engagement at the hinge end and the complementary coupling faces 28 into engagement at the latch end, coupling the first cam ring segment 22 and the second cam ring segment 24 into the coupled ring within the annular guide 18.

The operator then moves the latch 16 to its first position, in which the frame is held around the pipe 90 without clamping. The operator moves the latch handle 50 to the second, over-center position. The wedge 52 is driven against the ring drive face 36, the coupled ring turns through its stroke, the sides of the three oblique slots 34 drive the three followers 32, and the three jaw carriages 30 advance inwardly in synchronism until the pivoting jaw pads 40 seat on the pipe 90. The remaining travel of the latch handle 50 compresses the force-limiting spring stack 54, and the operator watches the indicator pin 56 move relative to the fixed edge of the latch housing 58 and so sees that the force-limiting spring stack 54 has entered the predetermined compression range. The latch 16 is left in the over-center position and the clamp 100 is loaded on the pipe 90.

To remove the clamp 100, the operator releases the latch 16. The latch handle 50 comes back over center, the wedge 52 retreats from the ring drive face 36, and the force-limiting spring stack 54 is unloaded. The carriage return springs 44 then push the jaw carriages 30 radially outward, so that the jaw pads 40 lift from the pipe 90. Only then are the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 swung apart about the hinge 14 and the clamp 100 taken off the pipe 90. The clamp 100 is undamaged by the cycle and may be installed again on the same pipe or on a pipe of a different diameter within the radial travel of the jaw carriages 30.

Features described above in connection with one embodiment may be combined with features described in connection with another, except where the context makes the combination impossible. The embodiments described are illustrative of the disclosed clamp and are not exhaustive of it, and the scope of protection is defined by the claims that follow rather than by any particular embodiment described here.

**Finding 1 — unsourced characterization in the Detailed Description.** Deleted the sentence about how a divided drive "must otherwise be operated separately in each half" and how the two halves then advance by amounts not fixed relative to one another. The paragraph now reads: "Coupling the segments in this way solves a problem created by splitting the clamp. Here the division of the ring is undone by the act of closing the clamp. In the closed condition ..." with the rest unchanged. The supported point survives intact in the sentences on either side, and `draft/05-background.md` is untouched, since that is where a characterization of the field properly sits.

**Finding 2 — claim 10's equipment element shown in no figure.** The equipment is now depicted and numbered:

- `figures/FIG-5.md`: a block rests on the upper end of the mounting boss 70 and is joined to it, drawn schematically as a plain rectangle in outline without hatching, identified as the equipment 80, with a broad interior leader target. I named it "an upper block" rather than repeating "a further block", which the mounting boss paragraph already uses, so the two solids cannot be confused, and noted that the name is a semantic identifier that does not appear as drawing text.

I also made the surrounding paragraph use the new part name consistently, since numeral discipline requires one part, one numeral, one set of words: "The mounting boss 70 supports equipment 80 that is to be held on the pipe 90 by the clamp 100" and "The equipment 80 carried at the mounting boss 70 therefore lies outside the drive path by which the jaws are advanced." The alternatives listed remain the inventor's own "a sensor, a tool, or a conduit", and the rectangular outline stays inside the figure brief as a depiction convention: no shape statement was added to the specification or claims.

All figure briefs remain within the character limit (2788, 2794, 2619, 2794, 1930). No em dash, TODO, TBD, placeholder, drafting note, or address to any person anywhere in `draft/` or `figures/`. reasoning: The deleted sentence was the only place in the Detailed Description making a factual claim about clamps other than the disclosed one. The following description of embodiments refers to the accompanying drawings. The same reference numeral denotes the same part throughout. Terms of direction are used with respect to the frame of the clamp: the axis of the frame is the axis about which the frame is annular in the closed condition, "inward" and "radially inward" mean toward that axis, "outward" and "radially outward" mean away from it, and "circumferential" means about that axis. These terms describe relationships within the clamp and do not require the clamp to be used in any particular attitude.

Overall arrangement

FIG. 1 shows a split pipe clamp 100 in the closed condition around a pipe 90. The clamp 100 has a first frame half 10 and a second frame half 12. Each of the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 is semicircular, and the two frame halves together surround the pipe 90. The first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 are joined at one end, referred to as the hinge end, by a hinge 14, and are releasably joined at the other end, referred to as the latch end, by a releasable latch 16. The hinge 14 permits the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 to be swung apart far enough for the frame halves to be placed around the pipe 90 from the side. When the frame halves are brought together and the latch 16 is engaged, the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 define a frame that is annular about the axis of the clamp 100.

Three jaw carriages 30 are distributed around the frame in the closed condition, so that the three jaw carriages 30 approach the pipe 90 from three different directions. Each jaw carriage 30 moves radially with respect to the frame and carries at its inner end a jaw pad 40, which is described below in connection with FIG. 3. The jaw pads 40 carried at the inner ends of the three jaw carriages 30 bear on the pipe 90 when the clamp 100 is clamped. The clamp 100 does not require a part dimensioned to a particular pipe diameter, and the same clamp 100 serves pipes of different diameters within the radial travel of the jaw carriages 30.

The frame may carry a mounting boss 70 outside the annular guide 18 described below, as shown in FIG. 5, which is taken on a plane corresponding to the plane of FIG. 3. The mounting boss 70 supports equipment 80 that is to be held on the pipe 90 by the clamp 100. FIG. 5 shows the equipment 80 supported on the mounting boss 70, the equipment 80 being a sensor, a tool, or a conduit. The mounting boss 70 does not participate in the advance of the three jaw carriages 30 inwardly in synchronism. The equipment 80 carried at the mounting boss 70 therefore lies outside the drive path by which the jaws are advanced. The mounting boss 70 is an optional feature of the clamp 100 and may be omitted.

The segmented cam ring

FIG. 2 shows the segmented cam ring 20 of the clamp 100, drawn removed from the frame with its segments in the coupled condition. The segmented cam ring 20 comprises a first cam ring segment 22 and a second cam ring segment 24. The first cam ring segment 22 is carried by the first frame half 10 and the second cam ring segment 24 is carried by the second frame half 12, so that each frame half carries one segment of the ring and each segment travels with its own frame half when the clamp 100 is opened.

The first cam ring segment 22 and the second cam ring segment 24 meet at two places, one at the hinge end and one at the latch end. At the hinge end the two segments have complementary coupling faces 26, and at the latch end they have complementary coupling faces 28. The complementary coupling faces 26 and the complementary coupling faces 28 are circumferentially facing coupling faces, each pair being shaped so that one segment can transmit circumferential force to the other through the joint. The faces are brought into engagement by the same motion that closes the frame halves: as the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 are swung together about the hinge 14 and the latch 16 is engaged, the complementary coupling faces 26 close on one another at the hinge end and the complementary coupling faces 28 close on one another at the latch end.

Coupling the segments in this way solves a problem created by splitting the clamp. Here the division of the ring is undone by the act of closing the clamp. In the closed condition the first cam ring segment 22 and the second cam ring segment 24 are coupled at both ends and rotate together in the annular guide as a coupled ring, and a circumferential input applied to either segment is carried around the whole ring. One input, applied at one point on one frame half, therefore reaches every jaw carriage 30 through a single kinematic element, and the relationship between the jaw carriages 30 is set by the geometry of the ring rather than by the way the clamp is operated. When the latch 16 is released and the frame halves are swung apart, the complementary coupling faces 26 and the complementary coupling faces 28 separate and each segment stays with its own frame half, so that the coupling is made and broken by the closing and opening of the frame halves.

The segmented cam ring 20 has three oblique slots 34, one for each jaw carriage 30. Each oblique slot 34 is inclined to the radial direction of the frame at the circumferential position of that slot, so that rotation of the coupled ring produces inward travel of its jaw carriage 30, the three oblique slots 34 being arranged so that the three jaw carriages 30 travel inwardly in synchronism. The inclination of the oblique slots 34 sets the ratio between the circumferential stroke of the coupled ring and the radial travel of the jaw carriages 30.

The segmented cam ring 20 further has a ring drive face 36, shown in FIG. 2 at the latch end of the ring, against which the latch acts as described below. The ring drive face 36 is presented at a position on the ring that the wedge of the latch can reach, and it lies at an inclination to the direction in which that wedge advances, so that advance of the wedge moves the segmented cam ring 20 circumferentially.

The jaw carriages

FIG. 3 is a fragmentary sectional view through one jaw carriage 30, taken along line 3-3 of FIG. 1. The frame is channeled to form the annular guide 18, which receives the segmented cam ring 20. The annular guide 18 retains the first cam ring segment 22 on the first frame half 10 and the second cam ring segment 24 on the second frame half 12, and permits the coupled ring to move circumferentially.

The frame is further formed with a radial guide 38 at the position of each jaw carriage 30. Each jaw carriage 30 is received in a respective radial guide 38 and is constrained by the radial guide 38 to move radially with respect to the frame. Each jaw carriage 30 carries a follower 32 that projects from the jaw carriage 30 into a respective one of the oblique slots 34 of the segmented cam ring 20. The follower 32 bears against the sides of the oblique slot 34.

The follower 32 is constrained in two ways at once. The radial guide 38 prevents the jaw carriage 30, and therefore the follower 32, from moving circumferentially, while the oblique slot 34 holds the follower 32 at a position along the slot, which is inclined to the radial direction, so that circumferential movement of the segmented cam ring 20 displaces the follower 32 radially. When the coupled ring turns through its stroke, the side of each oblique slot 34 bears on the corresponding follower 32 and drives it, and with it the jaw carriage 30, radially inward along the radial guide 38. Because all three followers 32 are engaged in oblique slots 34 of one coupled ring, the three jaw carriages 30 advance inwardly in synchronism for as long as the ring turns. The jaw pads 40 therefore close on the pipe together.

At its inner end each jaw carriage 30 carries a jaw pad 40. The jaw pad 40 is pivotally mounted on the jaw carriage 30 and has a concave bearing face directed inwardly of the frame. Because the jaw pad 40 is free to pivot on the jaw carriage 30, the concave bearing face aligns itself with the outer surface of the pipe as it lands. The same concave bearing face therefore seats on pipes of different diameters, and no part dimensioned to a particular pipe diameter is required.

A carriage return spring 44 acts on each jaw carriage 30 so as to urge that jaw carriage 30 radially outward. When the latch 16 is released and the drive from the latch to the ring drive face 36 is removed, the carriage return springs 44 push the jaw carriages 30 outward and the jaw pads 40 are retracted from the pipe, and the clamp 100 is left with its jaw carriages 30 retracted and ready for the next installation. Retraction of the jaw carriages 30 clears the jaw pads 40 from the pipe before the frame halves are swung apart.

The latch and the force-limiting drive train

FIG. 4 is an enlarged fragmentary view of the latch end, with parts shown in section. The latch 16 includes a latch housing 58 at the latch end, a latch handle 50, a wedge 52, and a force-limiting spring stack 54 in the drive train between the latch handle 50 and the wedge 52. The latch housing 58 presents a fixed edge referred to below in connection with the indicator pin 56. The wedge 52 is positioned so that its inclined face bears on the ring drive face 36 of the segmented cam ring 20.

The latch 16 has two engaged positions. In a first position, the latch 16 holds the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 closed around the pipe 90 but does not clamp it: the frame is captive on the pipe 90 and cannot fall away, while the segmented cam ring 20 has not yet advanced the jaw carriages 30. In a second, over-center position, the wedge 52 drives the segmented cam ring 20 and the pipe 90 is clamped. Movement of the latch handle 50 from the first position to the second position advances the wedge 52 against the ring drive face 36. The inclined face of the wedge 52 converts that advance into circumferential movement of the segmented cam ring 20, and the coupled ring turns through its limited stroke.

The force-limiting spring stack 54 answers the problem of what becomes of the operator's remaining handle travel. The jaw pads 40 land on the pipe 90 at some point in the stroke that depends on the diameter of the pipe 90, and the latch handle 50 has still to be carried into its over-center position. If the drive train from the latch handle 50 to the wedge 52 were rigid, that remaining travel would be taken up by whatever part of the assembly yielded first, in practice by driving one jaw farther into the pipe 90 than the others and loading it far more heavily. Additional travel of the latch handle 50 after all three jaw pads 40 have contacted the pipe 90 compresses the force-limiting spring stack 54 rather than forcing one jaw carriage 30 farther inward than the others.

An indicator pin 56 is coupled to the force-limiting spring stack 54 and projects from the latch housing 58. As the force-limiting spring stack 54 compresses, the indicator pin 56 moves relative to a fixed edge of the latch housing 58, and the position of the indicator pin 56 with respect to that fixed edge shows the operator when the force-limiting spring stack 54 has entered a predetermined compression range. The indicator pin 56 therefore reports clamp loading mechanically, and what it reports is the state of the force-limiting spring stack 54. It is not a measurement of the diameter of the pipe 90.

Operation

To install the clamp 100 on a pipe 90, the operator opens the latch 16 and swings the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 apart about the hinge 14. The first cam ring segment 22 stays with the first frame half 10 and the second cam ring segment 24 stays with the second frame half 12, and the complementary coupling faces 26 and the complementary coupling faces 28 are separated. The operator places the frame halves around the pipe 90 from the side and closes them about the hinge 14. Closing the frame halves brings the complementary coupling faces 26 into engagement at the hinge end and the complementary coupling faces 28 into engagement at the latch end, coupling the first cam ring segment 22 and the second cam ring segment 24 into the coupled ring within the annular guide 18.

The operator then moves the latch 16 to its first position, in which the frame is held around the pipe 90 without clamping. The operator moves the latch handle 50 to the second, over-center position. The wedge 52 is driven against the ring drive face 36, the coupled ring turns through its stroke, the sides of the three oblique slots 34 drive the three followers 32, and the three jaw carriages 30 advance inwardly in synchronism until the pivoting jaw pads 40 seat on the pipe 90. The remaining travel of the latch handle 50 compresses the force-limiting spring stack 54, and the operator watches the indicator pin 56 move relative to the fixed edge of the latch housing 58 and so sees that the force-limiting spring stack 54 has entered the predetermined compression range. The latch 16 is left in the over-center position and the clamp 100 is loaded on the pipe 90.

To remove the clamp 100, the operator releases the latch 16. The latch handle 50 comes back over center, the wedge 52 retreats from the ring drive face 36, and the force-limiting spring stack 54 is unloaded. The carriage return springs 44 then push the jaw carriages 30 radially outward, so that the jaw pads 40 lift from the pipe 90. Only then are the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 swung apart about the hinge 14 and the clamp 100 taken off the pipe 90. The clamp 100 is undamaged by the cycle and may be installed again on the same pipe or on a pipe of a different diameter within the radial travel of the jaw carriages 30.

Features described above in connection with one embodiment may be combined with features described in connection with another, except where the context makes the combination impossible. The embodiments described are illustrative of the disclosed clamp and are not exhaustive of it, and the scope of protection is defined by the claims that follow rather than by any particular embodiment described here.

The following description of embodiments refers to the accompanying drawings. The same reference numeral denotes the same part throughout. Terms of direction are used with respect to the frame of the clamp: the axis of the frame is the axis about which the frame is annular in the closed condition, "inward" and "radially inward" mean toward that axis, "outward" and "radially outward" mean away from it, and "circumferential" means about that axis. These terms describe relationships within the clamp and do not require the clamp to be used in any particular attitude.

Overall arrangement

FIG. 1 shows a split pipe clamp 100 in the closed condition around a pipe 90. The clamp 100 has a first frame half 10 and a second frame half 12. Each of the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 is semicircular, and the two frame halves together surround the pipe 90. The first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 are joined at one end, referred to as the hinge end, by a hinge 14, and are releasably joined at the other end, referred to as the latch end, by a releasable latch 16. The hinge 14 permits the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 to be swung apart far enough for the frame halves to be placed around the pipe 90 from the side. When the frame halves are brought together and the latch 16 is engaged, the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 define a frame that is annular about the axis of the clamp 100.

Three jaw carriages 30 are distributed around the frame in the closed condition, so that the three jaw carriages 30 approach the pipe 90 from three different directions. Each jaw carriage 30 moves radially with respect to the frame and carries at its inner end a jaw pad 40, which is described below in connection with FIG. 3. The jaw pads 40 carried at the inner ends of the three jaw carriages 30 bear on the pipe 90 when the clamp 100 is clamped. The clamp 100 does not require a part dimensioned to a particular pipe diameter, and the same clamp 100 serves pipes of different diameters within the radial travel of the jaw carriages 30.

The frame may carry a mounting boss 70 outside the annular guide 18 described below, as shown in FIG. 5, which is taken on a plane corresponding to the plane of FIG. 3. The mounting boss 70 supports equipment 80 that is to be held on the pipe 90 by the clamp 100. FIG. 5 shows the equipment 80 supported on the mounting boss 70, the equipment 80 being a sensor, a tool, or a conduit. The mounting boss 70 does not participate in the advance of the three jaw carriages 30 inwardly in synchronism. The equipment 80 carried at the mounting boss 70 therefore lies outside the drive path by which the jaws are advanced. The mounting boss 70 is an optional feature of the clamp 100 and may be omitted.

The segmented cam ring

FIG. 2 shows the segmented cam ring 20 of the clamp 100, drawn removed from the frame with its segments in the coupled condition. The segmented cam ring 20 comprises a first cam ring segment 22 and a second cam ring segment 24. The first cam ring segment 22 is carried by the first frame half 10 and the second cam ring segment 24 is carried by the second frame half 12, so that each frame half carries one segment of the ring and each segment travels with its own frame half when the clamp 100 is opened.

The first cam ring segment 22 and the second cam ring segment 24 meet at two places, one at the hinge end and one at the latch end. At the hinge end the two segments have complementary coupling faces 26, and at the latch end they have complementary coupling faces 28. The complementary coupling faces 26 and the complementary coupling faces 28 are each shaped so that one segment can transmit circumferential force to the other through the joint. The faces are brought into engagement by the same motion that closes the frame halves: as the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 are swung together about the hinge 14 and the latch 16 is engaged, the complementary coupling faces 26 close on one another at the hinge end and the complementary coupling faces 28 close on one another at the latch end.

Coupling the segments in this way solves a problem created by splitting the clamp. Here the division of the ring is undone by the act of closing the clamp. In the closed condition the first cam ring segment 22 and the second cam ring segment 24 are coupled at both ends and rotate together in the annular guide as a coupled ring, and a circumferential input applied to either segment is carried around the whole ring. One input, applied at one point on one frame half, therefore reaches every jaw carriage 30 through a single kinematic element, and the relationship between the jaw carriages 30 is set by the geometry of the ring rather than by the way the clamp is operated. When the latch 16 is released and the frame halves are swung apart, the complementary coupling faces 26 and the complementary coupling faces 28 separate and each segment stays with its own frame half, so that the coupling is made and broken by the closing and opening of the frame halves.

The segmented cam ring 20 has three oblique slots 34, one for each jaw carriage 30. Each oblique slot 34 is inclined to the radial direction of the frame at the circumferential position of that slot, so that rotation of the coupled ring produces inward travel of its jaw carriage 30, the three oblique slots 34 being arranged so that the three jaw carriages 30 travel inwardly in synchronism. The inclination of the oblique slots 34 sets the ratio between the circumferential stroke of the coupled ring and the radial travel of the jaw carriages 30.

The segmented cam ring 20 further has a ring drive face 36, shown in FIG. 2 at the latch end of the ring, against which the latch acts as described below. The ring drive face 36 is presented at a position on the ring that the wedge of the latch can reach, and it lies at an inclination to the direction in which that wedge advances, so that advance of the wedge moves the segmented cam ring 20 circumferentially.

The jaw carriages

FIG. 3 is a fragmentary sectional view through one jaw carriage 30, taken along line 3-3 of FIG. 1. The frame is channeled to form the annular guide 18, which receives the segmented cam ring 20. The annular guide 18 retains the first cam ring segment 22 on the first frame half 10 and the second cam ring segment 24 on the second frame half 12, and permits the coupled ring to move circumferentially.

The frame is further formed with a radial guide 38 at the position of each jaw carriage 30. Each jaw carriage 30 is received in a respective radial guide 38 and is constrained by the radial guide 38 to move radially with respect to the frame. Each jaw carriage 30 carries a follower 32 that projects from the jaw carriage 30 into a respective one of the oblique slots 34 of the segmented cam ring 20. The follower 32 bears against the sides of the oblique slot 34.

The follower 32 is constrained in two ways at once. The radial guide 38 prevents the jaw carriage 30, and therefore the follower 32, from moving circumferentially, while the oblique slot 34 holds the follower 32 at a position along the slot, which is inclined to the radial direction, so that circumferential movement of the segmented cam ring 20 displaces the follower 32 radially. When the coupled ring turns through its stroke, the side of each oblique slot 34 bears on the corresponding follower 32 and drives it, and with it the jaw carriage 30, radially inward along the radial guide 38. Because all three followers 32 are engaged in oblique slots 34 of one coupled ring, the three jaw carriages 30 advance inwardly in synchronism for as long as the ring turns. The jaw pads 40 therefore close on the pipe together.

At its inner end each jaw carriage 30 carries a jaw pad 40. The jaw pad 40 is pivotally mounted on the jaw carriage 30 and has a concave bearing face directed inwardly of the frame. Because the jaw pad 40 is free to pivot on the jaw carriage 30, the concave bearing face aligns itself with the outer surface of the pipe as it lands. The same concave bearing face therefore seats on pipes of different diameters, and no part dimensioned to a particular pipe diameter is required.

A carriage return spring 44 acts on each jaw carriage 30 so as to urge that jaw carriage 30 radially outward. When the latch 16 is released and the drive from the latch to the ring drive face 36 is removed, the carriage return springs 44 push the jaw carriages 30 outward and the jaw pads 40 are retracted from the pipe, and the clamp 100 is left with its jaw carriages 30 retracted and ready for the next installation. Retraction of the jaw carriages 30 clears the jaw pads 40 from the pipe before the frame halves are swung apart.

The latch and the force-limiting drive train

FIG. 4 is an enlarged fragmentary view of the latch end, with parts shown in section. The latch 16 includes a latch housing 58 at the latch end, a latch handle 50, a wedge 52, and a force-limiting spring stack 54 in the drive train between the latch handle 50 and the wedge 52. The latch housing 58 presents a fixed edge referred to below in connection with the indicator pin 56. The wedge 52 is positioned so that its inclined face bears on the ring drive face 36 of the segmented cam ring 20.

The latch 16 has two engaged positions. In a first position, the latch 16 holds the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 closed around the pipe 90 but does not clamp it: the frame is captive on the pipe 90 and cannot fall away, while the segmented cam ring 20 has not yet advanced the jaw carriages 30. In a second, over-center position, the wedge 52 drives the segmented cam ring 20 and the pipe 90 is clamped. Movement of the latch handle 50 from the first position to the second position advances the wedge 52 against the ring drive face 36. The inclined face of the wedge 52 converts that advance into circumferential movement of the segmented cam ring 20, and the coupled ring turns through its limited stroke.

The force-limiting spring stack 54 answers the problem of what becomes of the operator's remaining handle travel. The jaw pads 40 land on the pipe 90 at some point in the stroke that depends on the diameter of the pipe 90, and the latch handle 50 has still to be carried into its over-center position. If the drive train from the latch handle 50 to the wedge 52 were rigid, that remaining travel would be taken up by whatever part of the assembly yielded first, in practice by driving one jaw farther into the pipe 90 than the others and loading it far more heavily. Additional travel of the latch handle 50 after all three jaw pads 40 have contacted the pipe 90 compresses the force-limiting spring stack 54 rather than forcing one jaw carriage 30 farther inward than the others.

An indicator pin 56 is coupled to the force-limiting spring stack 54 and projects from the latch housing 58. As the force-limiting spring stack 54 compresses, the indicator pin 56 moves relative to a fixed edge of the latch housing 58, and the position of the indicator pin 56 with respect to that fixed edge shows the operator when the force-limiting spring stack 54 has entered a predetermined compression range. The indicator pin 56 therefore reports clamp loading mechanically, and what it reports is the state of the force-limiting spring stack 54. It is not a measurement of the diameter of the pipe 90.

Operation

To install the clamp 100 on a pipe 90, the operator opens the latch 16 and swings the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 apart about the hinge 14. The first cam ring segment 22 stays with the first frame half 10 and the second cam ring segment 24 stays with the second frame half 12, and the complementary coupling faces 26 and the complementary coupling faces 28 are separated. The operator places the frame halves around the pipe 90 from the side and closes them about the hinge 14. Closing the frame halves brings the complementary coupling faces 26 into engagement at the hinge end and the complementary coupling faces 28 into engagement at the latch end, coupling the first cam ring segment 22 and the second cam ring segment 24 into the coupled ring within the annular guide 18.

The operator then moves the latch 16 to its first position, in which the frame is held around the pipe 90 without clamping. The operator moves the latch handle 50 to the second, over-center position. The wedge 52 is driven against the ring drive face 36, the coupled ring turns through its stroke, the sides of the three oblique slots 34 drive the three followers 32, and the three jaw carriages 30 advance inwardly in synchronism until the pivoting jaw pads 40 seat on the pipe 90. The remaining travel of the latch handle 50 compresses the force-limiting spring stack 54, and the operator watches the indicator pin 56 move relative to the fixed edge of the latch housing 58 and so sees that the force-limiting spring stack 54 has entered the predetermined compression range. The latch 16 is left in the over-center position and the clamp 100 is loaded on the pipe 90.

To remove the clamp 100, the operator releases the latch 16. The latch handle 50 comes back over center, the wedge 52 retreats from the ring drive face 36, and the force-limiting spring stack 54 is unloaded. The carriage return springs 44 then push the jaw carriages 30 radially outward, so that the jaw pads 40 lift from the pipe 90. Only then are the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 swung apart about the hinge 14 and the clamp 100 taken off the pipe 90. The clamp 100 is undamaged by the cycle and may be installed again on the same pipe or on a pipe of a different diameter within the radial travel of the jaw carriages 30.

Features described above in connection with one embodiment may be combined with features described in connection with another, except where the context makes the combination impossible. The embodiments described are illustrative of the disclosed clamp and are not exhaustive of it, and the scope of protection is defined by the claims that follow rather than by any particular embodiment described here.

That post is the follower 32.

At the left joint the ends of the first cam ring segment 22 and the second cam ring segment 24 meet along complementary surfaces facing circumferentially, the complementary coupling faces at the hinge end 26.

At the right joint the two segment ends meet in the same way, along complementary surfaces facing circumferentially, the complementary coupling faces at the latch end 28.

content.text:
All five findings are fixed.

**Two major items**

1. `draft/08-detailed-description.md` — the coupling faces are no longer given an orientation. The sentence now reads: "The complementary coupling faces 26 and the complementary coupling faces 28 are each shaped so that one segment can transmit circumferential force to the other through the joint." The functional relationship the inventor stated survives; the "circumferentially facing" form stays in the FIG. 2 brief, where it is already labelled schematic, and `figures/FIG-2.md` was left with that depiction intact.
2. `figures/FIG-3.md` — the schematic sentence in the opening note now covers the follower-and-guide topology: "The carriage return spring and its seats, the direction in which the follower 32 projects, the direction in which the annular guide 18 opens, the passage of the oblique slot 34 through the segmented cam ring 20, and the meeting of the radial guide 38 with the mouth of the annular guide 18 are shown schematically." `figures/FIG-5.md` now hedges the groove's opening direction as well as its proportions. The Detailed Description was left direction-neutral and unchanged on these relationships.

**Three minor items**

3. "The frame is channeled to form the annular guide 18" is now "The frame is formed with the annular guide 18", matching claim 6's shape-neutral wording.
4. The Operation section's closing sentence now reads "The clamp 100 may be installed again on the same pipe or on a pipe of a different diameter within the radial travel of the jaw carriages 30", dropping the asserted result that the clamp is undamaged by the cycle.
5. `figures/FIG-2.md` line 13 now ends "; that handedness and the corresponding sense of ring rotation are shown schematically." The geometry is unchanged, so FIG. 2 and FIG. 4 stay kinematically consistent.

**Length management.** The added hedges would have pushed FIG. 2 to about 2899 and FIG. 3 to about 2887 characters, over the 2800 limit, so I paid for them by removing invented rendering constraints rather than disclosed content: the outline-stroke instruction on the cam ring block ("leaving a portion of its outline above the opening and a portion below it"), a duplicate hedge on the spring seats now carried by the opening note, "as viewed here", a repeated face description at the right joint that "in the same way" already imports, and two short redundancies. Every body, contact, opening, clearance, engagement, and numeral target survives. Final sizes: 2788, 2786, 2778, 2794, 1945.

**Verification.** The numeral table still holds 26 unique entries, all used in the text and each on at least one sheet, with no sheet over eight. Claims, Summary, Abstract, and Background are untouched this pass. No em dash, TODO, TBD, placeholder, drafting note, or address to any person anywhere in `draft/` or `figures/`.

input.summary: Fixed all five findings. The Detailed Description no longer commits to a circumferentially facing form for coupling faces 26 and 28; it now recites only that each pair is shaped so one segment can transmit circumferential force to the other through the joint, leaving the depiction in the FIG. 2 brief where it is already labelled schematic. The FIG. 3 brief's schematic sentence now covers the follower projection direction, the direction in which the annular guide 18 opens, the passage of the oblique slot 34 through the segmented cam ring 20, and the meeting of the radial guide 38 with the mouth of the annular guide 18, and FIG. 5 now hedges the groove's opening direction as well as its proportions. The description's channeled shape assertion became formed with, matching claim 6's shape-neutral wording. The asserted result that the clamp is undamaged by the cycle was deleted, leaving the supported statement that the clamp may be installed again on the same pipe or on a pipe of a different diameter within the radial travel of the jaw carriages. The FIG. 2 brief now marks the slot handedness and the corresponding sense of ring rotation as shown schematically, with no geometry changed, so FIG. 2 and FIG. 4 remain kinematically consistent. The added hedges would have taken FIG. 2 and FIG. 3 over the 2800-character limit, so I removed invented rendering constraints to pay for them: an outline-stroke instruction on the cam ring block, a duplicated spring-seat hedge, and three short redundancies. Final brief sizes are 2788, 2786, 2778, 2794 and 1945. The numeral table still holds 26 unique entries, each used in the text and shown on at least one sheet with no sheet over eight, and the claims, Summary, Abstract and Background were not touched.
reasoning: The coupling-face finding was the important one because the leak ran the wrong way through the authority order. The FIG. 2 brief had already conceded that the form of the meeting surfaces is a depiction choice, and the description then stated that same choice as fact. Removing 'circumferentially facing' from the description costs nothing: what the invention needs is that the pair transmits circumferential force through the joint when the halves close, which is exactly what the inventor states functionally and what the surviving clause says. Claims 1, 7, 10 and 13 already recite only complementary coupling faces, so the description now matches the claims instead of running ahead of them.

The FIG. 3 topology items are connection facts, not outlines, which is why they needed hedging rather than deletion. Which way the follower projects, which way the annular guide opens, whether the slot is a through opening, and how the radial guide meets the guide mouth all convey real technical substance that the inventor never specifies; but a sectional view cannot be drawn without picking one arrangement. Labelling them schematic keeps the drawing buildable while preventing a later reading that the invention requires an axially projecting follower. The description already recites these relationships in direction-neutral terms, so it needed no change and got none.

I hedged FIG. 5's groove opening direction too, because FIG. 5 repeats the same axially opening groove as FIG. 3 and an unhedged repeat would have reasserted the choice the FIG. 3 fix had just qualified.

Channeled had to go because it fixes a groove form in the application text while both briefs treat the groove as a schematic depiction, and because claim 6 recites the annular guide purely by what it does: retains the segments and permits circumferential movement of the coupled ring. Formed with leaves the guide defined by its function, which is how the inventor names it.

Undamaged by the cycle is an outcome, not a restatement of reusable. Reusability is supported and is retained through the surviving sentence about reinstalling on the same pipe or on a pipe of a different diameter within the jaw travel. An unsupported durability claim in the description is exactly the kind of asserted result that cannot be traced to any inventor passage, so deleting it removes risk without narrowing anything.

The FIG. 2 handedness choice is forced: a drawing must pick one of the two senses, and the one already chosen is internally correct, since clockwise rotation of the depicted slots carries the followers inward and agrees with the wedge driving the band leftward in the mirrored FIG. 4 view. So I labelled the choice rather than touching the geometry. Changing the handedness would have broken the consistency between FIG. 2 and FIG. 4 that earlier review passes verified, and the description and claims are already neutral as to the sense of rotation.

The hedges cost characters, and I refused to pay for them out of disclosed content. What I cut instead was the sort of thing the drafting rules say does not belong in a brief anyway: an instruction about how much of the block outline to leave above and below the opening, which is a linework control rather than physical geometry, a spring-seat hedge that the opening note now carries, a repeated face description at the right joint that 'in the same way' already imports, and two short redundancies. Every solid, contact, clearance, opening, engagement and numeral target is intact, and the numeral distribution across sheets is unchanged.

structured_output.summary: Fixed all five findings. The Detailed Description no longer commits to a circumferentially facing form for coupling faces 26 and 28; it now recites only that each pair is shaped so one segment can transmit circumferential force to the other through the joint, leaving the depiction in the FIG. 2 brief where it is already labelled schematic. The FIG. 3 brief's schematic sentence now covers the follower projection direction, the direction in which the annular guide 18 opens, the passage of the oblique slot 34 through the segmented cam ring 20, and the meeting of the radial guide 38 with the mouth of the annular guide 18, and FIG. 5 now hedges the groove's opening direction as well as its proportions. The description's channeled shape assertion became formed with, matching claim 6's shape-neutral wording. The asserted result that the clamp is undamaged by the cycle was deleted, leaving the supported statement that the clamp may be installed again on the same pipe or on a pipe of a different diameter within the radial travel of the jaw carriages. The FIG. 2 brief now marks the slot handedness and the corresponding sense of ring rotation as shown schematically, with no geometry changed, so FIG. 2 and FIG. 4 remain kinematically consistent. The added hedges would have taken FIG. 2 and FIG. 3 over the 2800-character limit, so I removed invented rendering constraints to pay for them: an outline-stroke instruction on the cam ring block, a duplicated spring-seat hedge, and three short redundancies. Final brief sizes are 2788, 2786, 2778, 2794 and 1945. The numeral table still holds 26 unique entries, each used in the text and shown on at least one sheet with no sheet over eight, and the claims, Summary, Abstract and Background were not touched.
reasoning: The coupling-face finding was the important one because the leak ran the wrong way through the authority order. The FIG. 2 brief had already conceded that the form of the meeting surfaces is a depiction choice, and the description then stated that same choice as fact. Removing 'circumferentially facing' from the description costs nothing: what the invention needs is that the pair transmits circumferential force through the joint when the halves close, which is exactly what the inventor states functionally and what the surviving clause says. Claims 1, 7, 10 and 13 already recite only complementary coupling faces, so the description now matches the claims instead of running ahead of them.

The FIG. 3 topology items are connection facts, not outlines, which is why they needed hedging rather than deletion. Which way the follower projects, which way the annular guide opens, whether the slot is a through opening, and how the radial guide meets the guide mouth all convey real technical substance that the inventor never specifies; but a sectional view cannot be drawn without picking one arrangement. Labelling them schematic keeps the drawing buildable while preventing a later reading that the invention requires an axially projecting follower. The description already recites these relationships in direction-neutral terms, so it needed no change and got none.

I hedged FIG. 5's groove opening direction too, because FIG. 5 repeats the same axially opening groove as FIG. 3 and an unhedged repeat would have reasserted the choice the FIG. 3 fix had just qualified.

Channeled had to go because it fixes a groove form in the application text while both briefs treat the groove as a schematic depiction, and because claim 6 recites the annular guide purely by what it does: retains the segments and permits circumferential movement of the coupled ring. Formed with leaves the guide defined by its function, which is how the inventor names it.

Undamaged by the cycle is an outcome, not a restatement of reusable. Reusability is supported and is retained through the surviving sentence about reinstalling on the same pipe or on a pipe of a different diameter within the jaw travel. An unsupported durability claim in the description is exactly the kind of asserted result that cannot be traced to any inventor passage, so deleting it removes risk without narrowing anything.

The FIG. 2 handedness choice is forced: a drawing must pick one of the two senses, and the one already chosen is internally correct, since clockwise rotation of the depicted slots carries the followers inward and agrees with the wedge driving the band leftward in the mirrored FIG. 4 view. So I labelled the choice rather than touching the geometry. Changing the handedness would have broken the consistency between FIG. 2 and FIG. 4 that earlier review passes verified, and the description and claims are already neutral as to the sense of rotation.

The hedges cost characters, and I refused to pay for them out of disclosed content. What I cut instead was the sort of thing the drafting rules say does not belong in a brief anyway: an instruction about how much of the block outline to leave above and below the opening, which is a linework control rather than physical geometry, a spring-seat hedge that the opening note now carries, a repeated face description at the right joint that 'in the same way' already imports, and two short redundancies. Every solid, contact, clearance, opening, engagement and numeral target is intact, and the numeral distribution across sheets is unchanged.

The following description of embodiments refers to the accompanying drawings. The same reference numeral denotes the same part throughout. Terms of direction are used with respect to the frame of the clamp: the axis of the frame is the axis about which the frame is annular in the closed condition, "inward" and "radially inward" mean toward that axis, "outward" and "radially outward" mean away from it, and "circumferential" means about that axis. These terms describe relationships within the clamp and do not require the clamp to be used in any particular attitude.

Overall arrangement

FIG. 1 shows a split pipe clamp 100 in the closed condition around a pipe 90. The clamp 100 has a first frame half 10 and a second frame half 12. Each of the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 is semicircular, and the two frame halves together surround the pipe 90. The first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 are joined at one end, referred to as the hinge end, by a hinge 14, and are releasably joined at the other end, referred to as the latch end, by a releasable latch 16. The hinge 14 permits the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 to be swung apart far enough for the frame halves to be placed around the pipe 90 from the side. When the frame halves are brought together and the latch 16 is engaged, the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 define a frame that is annular about the axis of the clamp 100.

Three jaw carriages 30 are distributed around the frame in the closed condition, so that the three jaw carriages 30 approach the pipe 90 from three different directions. Each jaw carriage 30 moves radially with respect to the frame and carries at its inner end a jaw pad 40, which is described below in connection with FIG. 3. The jaw pads 40 carried at the inner ends of the three jaw carriages 30 bear on the pipe 90 when the clamp 100 is clamped. The clamp 100 does not require a part dimensioned to a particular pipe diameter, and the same clamp 100 serves pipes of different diameters within the radial travel of the jaw carriages 30.

The frame may carry a mounting boss 70 outside the annular guide 18 described below, as shown in FIG. 5, which is taken on a plane corresponding to the plane of FIG. 3. The mounting boss 70 supports equipment 80 that is to be held on the pipe 90 by the clamp 100. FIG. 5 shows the equipment 80 supported on the mounting boss 70, the equipment 80 being a sensor, a tool, or a conduit. The mounting boss 70 does not participate in the advance of the three jaw carriages 30 inwardly in synchronism. The equipment 80 carried at the mounting boss 70 therefore lies outside the drive path by which the jaws are advanced. The mounting boss 70 is an optional feature of the clamp 100 and may be omitted.

The segmented cam ring

FIG. 2 shows the segmented cam ring 20 of the clamp 100, drawn removed from the frame with its segments in the coupled condition. The segmented cam ring 20 comprises a first cam ring segment 22 and a second cam ring segment 24. The first cam ring segment 22 is carried by the first frame half 10 and the second cam ring segment 24 is carried by the second frame half 12, so that each frame half carries one segment of the ring and each segment travels with its own frame half when the clamp 100 is opened.

The first cam ring segment 22 and the second cam ring segment 24 meet at two places, one at the hinge end and one at the latch end. At the hinge end the two segments have complementary coupling faces 26, and at the latch end they have complementary coupling faces 28. The complementary coupling faces 26 and the complementary coupling faces 28 are each shaped so that one segment can transmit circumferential force to the other through the joint. The faces are brought into engagement by the same motion that closes the frame halves: as the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 are swung together about the hinge 14 and the latch 16 is engaged, the complementary coupling faces 26 close on one another at the hinge end and the complementary coupling faces 28 close on one another at the latch end.

Coupling the segments in this way solves a problem created by splitting the clamp. Here the division of the ring is undone by the act of closing the clamp. In the closed condition the first cam ring segment 22 and the second cam ring segment 24 are coupled at both ends and rotate together in the annular guide as a coupled ring, and a circumferential input applied to either segment is carried around the whole ring. One input, applied at one point on one frame half, therefore reaches every jaw carriage 30 through a single kinematic element, and the relationship between the jaw carriages 30 is set by the geometry of the ring rather than by the way the clamp is operated. When the latch 16 is released and the frame halves are swung apart, the complementary coupling faces 26 and the complementary coupling faces 28 separate and each segment stays with its own frame half, so that the coupling is made and broken by the closing and opening of the frame halves.

The segmented cam ring 20 has three oblique slots 34, one for each jaw carriage 30. Each oblique slot 34 is inclined to the radial direction of the frame at the circumferential position of that slot, so that rotation of the coupled ring produces inward travel of its jaw carriage 30, the three oblique slots 34 being arranged so that the three jaw carriages 30 travel inwardly in synchronism. The inclination of the oblique slots 34 sets the ratio between the circumferential stroke of the coupled ring and the radial travel of the jaw carriages 30.

The segmented cam ring 20 further has a ring drive face 36, shown in FIG. 2 at the latch end of the ring, against which the latch acts as described below. The ring drive face 36 is presented at a position on the ring that the wedge of the latch can reach, and it lies at an inclination to the direction in which that wedge advances, so that advance of the wedge moves the segmented cam ring 20 circumferentially.

The jaw carriages

FIG. 3 is a fragmentary sectional view through one jaw carriage 30, taken along line 3-3 of FIG. 1. The frame is formed with the annular guide 18, which receives the segmented cam ring 20. The annular guide 18 retains the first cam ring segment 22 on the first frame half 10 and the second cam ring segment 24 on the second frame half 12, and permits the coupled ring to move circumferentially.

The frame is further formed with a radial guide 38 at the position of each jaw carriage 30. Each jaw carriage 30 is received in a respective radial guide 38 and is constrained by the radial guide 38 to move radially with respect to the frame. Each jaw carriage 30 carries a follower 32 that projects from the jaw carriage 30 into a respective one of the oblique slots 34 of the segmented cam ring 20. The follower 32 bears against the sides of the oblique slot 34.

The follower 32 is constrained in two ways at once. The radial guide 38 prevents the jaw carriage 30, and therefore the follower 32, from moving circumferentially, while the oblique slot 34 holds the follower 32 at a position along the slot, which is inclined to the radial direction, so that circumferential movement of the segmented cam ring 20 displaces the follower 32 radially. When the coupled ring turns through its stroke, the side of each oblique slot 34 bears on the corresponding follower 32 and drives it, and with it the jaw carriage 30, radially inward along the radial guide 38. Because all three followers 32 are engaged in oblique slots 34 of one coupled ring, the three jaw carriages 30 advance inwardly in synchronism for as long as the ring turns. The jaw pads 40 therefore close on the pipe together.

At its inner end each jaw carriage 30 carries a jaw pad 40. The jaw pad 40 is pivotally mounted on the jaw carriage 30 and has a concave bearing face directed inwardly of the frame. Because the jaw pad 40 is free to pivot on the jaw carriage 30, the concave bearing face aligns itself with the outer surface of the pipe as it lands. The same concave bearing face therefore seats on pipes of different diameters, and no part dimensioned to a particular pipe diameter is required.

A carriage return spring 44 acts on each jaw carriage 30 so as to urge that jaw carriage 30 radially outward. When the latch 16 is released and the drive from the latch to the ring drive face 36 is removed, the carriage return springs 44 push the jaw carriages 30 outward and the jaw pads 40 are retracted from the pipe, and the clamp 100 is left with its jaw carriages 30 retracted and ready for the next installation. Retraction of the jaw carriages 30 clears the jaw pads 40 from the pipe before the frame halves are swung apart.

The latch and the force-limiting drive train

FIG. 4 is an enlarged fragmentary view of the latch end, with parts shown in section. The latch 16 includes a latch housing 58 at the latch end, a latch handle 50, a wedge 52, and a force-limiting spring stack 54 in the drive train between the latch handle 50 and the wedge 52. The latch housing 58 presents a fixed edge referred to below in connection with the indicator pin 56. The wedge 52 is positioned so that its inclined face bears on the ring drive face 36 of the segmented cam ring 20.

The latch 16 has two engaged positions. In a first position, the latch 16 holds the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 closed around the pipe 90 but does not clamp it: the frame is captive on the pipe 90 and cannot fall away, while the segmented cam ring 20 has not yet advanced the jaw carriages 30. In a second, over-center position, the wedge 52 drives the segmented cam ring 20 and the pipe 90 is clamped. Movement of the latch handle 50 from the first position to the second position advances the wedge 52 against the ring drive face 36. The inclined face of the wedge 52 converts that advance into circumferential movement of the segmented cam ring 20, and the coupled ring turns through its limited stroke.

The force-limiting spring stack 54 answers the problem of what becomes of the operator's remaining handle travel. The jaw pads 40 land on the pipe 90 at some point in the stroke that depends on the diameter of the pipe 90, and the latch handle 50 has still to be carried into its over-center position. If the drive train from the latch handle 50 to the wedge 52 were rigid, that remaining travel would be taken up by whatever part of the assembly yielded first, in practice by driving one jaw farther into the pipe 90 than the others and loading it far more heavily. Additional travel of the latch handle 50 after all three jaw pads 40 have contacted the pipe 90 compresses the force-limiting spring stack 54 rather than forcing one jaw carriage 30 farther inward than the others.

An indicator pin 56 is coupled to the force-limiting spring stack 54 and projects from the latch housing 58. As the force-limiting spring stack 54 compresses, the indicator pin 56 moves relative to a fixed edge of the latch housing 58, and the position of the indicator pin 56 with respect to that fixed edge shows the operator when the force-limiting spring stack 54 has entered a predetermined compression range. The indicator pin 56 therefore reports clamp loading mechanically, and what it reports is the state of the force-limiting spring stack 54. It is not a measurement of the diameter of the pipe 90.

Operation

To install the clamp 100 on a pipe 90, the operator opens the latch 16 and swings the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 apart about the hinge 14. The first cam ring segment 22 stays with the first frame half 10 and the second cam ring segment 24 stays with the second frame half 12, and the complementary coupling faces 26 and the complementary coupling faces 28 are separated. The operator places the frame halves around the pipe 90 from the side and closes them about the hinge 14. Closing the frame halves brings the complementary coupling faces 26 into engagement at the hinge end and the complementary coupling faces 28 into engagement at the latch end, coupling the first cam ring segment 22 and the second cam ring segment 24 into the coupled ring within the annular guide 18.

The operator then moves the latch 16 to its first position, in which the frame is held around the pipe 90 without clamping. The operator moves the latch handle 50 to the second, over-center position. The wedge 52 is driven against the ring drive face 36, the coupled ring turns through its stroke, the sides of the three oblique slots 34 drive the three followers 32, and the three jaw carriages 30 advance inwardly in synchronism until the pivoting jaw pads 40 seat on the pipe 90. The remaining travel of the latch handle 50 compresses the force-limiting spring stack 54, and the operator watches the indicator pin 56 move relative to the fixed edge of the latch housing 58 and so sees that the force-limiting spring stack 54 has entered the predetermined compression range. The latch 16 is left in the over-center position and the clamp 100 is loaded on the pipe 90.

To remove the clamp 100, the operator releases the latch 16. The latch handle 50 comes back over center, the wedge 52 retreats from the ring drive face 36, and the force-limiting spring stack 54 is unloaded. The carriage return springs 44 then push the jaw carriages 30 radially outward, so that the jaw pads 40 lift from the pipe 90. Only then are the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 swung apart about the hinge 14 and the clamp 100 taken off the pipe 90. The clamp 100 may be installed again on the same pipe or on a pipe of a different diameter within the radial travel of the jaw carriages 30.

Features described above in connection with one embodiment may be combined with features described in connection with another, except where the context makes the combination impossible. The embodiments described are illustrative of the disclosed clamp and are not exhaustive of it, and the scope of protection is defined by the claims that follow rather than by any particular embodiment described here.

# FIG. 4

Enlarged fragmentary view of the latch end of the clamp, with parts shown in section, viewed along the axis of the frame from the side of the plane of FIG. 1 opposite to the side from which FIG. 1 is viewed. Radially outward is toward the top, the circumferential direction runs left to right, and the right of the view lies toward the first frame half; that orientation note is not a reference numeral and no numeral for the first frame half appears on this figure. Cut solid material carries section hatching; black line work on white, well inside the drawing area. Shown schematically: the latch housing and its cavity; the interruption of the frame wall radially outside the band at the latch end; the direction in which the wedge 52 advances; the force-limiting spring stack 54 drawn as one spring symbol; the mounting of the latch handle 50 to the latch housing 58, the gap through which it passes, and its linkage to that stack; and the opening in the top wall for the indicator pin 56 and its coupling to that stack.

At the lower left a hatched body in section holds a hatched arcuate band from the left, the segmented cam ring 20. The frame wall radially outside the band is interrupted at the latch end, exposing the band's upper side to the wedge 52. Near its right end that upper side runs as a short straight surface slanting downward to the right, the ring drive face 36.

To the right a hatched enclosure, the latch housing 58, has left, right and top walls enclosing a cavity opening downward above the band's right end.

A block, the wedge 52, lies in the cavity between those walls. Its lower left face slants at the same angle as the ring drive face 36 and bears on it, so downward movement drives the band left.

Above it the force-limiting spring stack 54 is a zigzag spring line rising from the wedge 52 into the cavity.

An elongated lever, the latch handle 50, is pivoted to the latch housing 58 at a small circle at the upper right of the cavity. From that pivot a short arm reaches down and left onto the upper end of that stack, and the lever runs up and right out through a gap between the top wall and the right wall, leaning right past upright, the over-center position.

A slender pin, the indicator pin 56, rises from that stack through a hole in the top wall.

## Numerals shown on this figure

- 16 latch: target the assembly as a whole, outside the enclosure.
- 20 segmented cam ring: target the hatching of the band.
- 36 ring drive face: target the slanting surface on the band.
- 50 latch handle: target well inside the lever.
- 52 wedge: target well inside the block in the cavity.
- 54 force-limiting spring stack: target the zigzag line.
- 56 indicator pin: target the pin above the top wall.
- 58 latch housing: target the hatching of the top wall.

# FIG. 4

Enlarged fragmentary view of the latch end of the clamp, with parts shown in section, viewed along the axis of the frame from the side of the plane of FIG. 1 opposite to the side from which FIG. 1 is viewed. Radially outward is toward the top, the circumferential direction runs left to right, and the right of the view lies toward the first frame half; that orientation note is not a reference numeral and no numeral for the first frame half appears on this figure. Cut solid material carries section hatching; black line work on white, well inside the drawing area. Shown schematically: the latch housing and its cavity; the interruption of the frame wall radially outside the band at the latch end; the direction in which the wedge 52 advances; the force-limiting spring stack 54 drawn as one spring symbol; the mounting of the latch handle 50 to the latch housing 58, the gap through which it passes, and its linkage to that stack; and the opening in the top wall for the indicator pin 56 and its coupling to that stack.

At the lower left a hatched body in section holds a hatched arcuate band from the left, the segmented cam ring 20. The frame wall radially outside the band is interrupted at the latch end, exposing the band's upper side to the wedge 52. Near its right end that upper side runs as a short straight surface slanting downward to the right, the ring drive face 36.

To the right a hatched enclosure, the latch housing 58, has left, right and top walls enclosing a cavity opening downward above the band's right end.

A block, the wedge 52, lies in the cavity between those walls. Its lower left face slants at the same angle as the ring drive face 36 and bears on it, so downward movement drives the band left.

Above it the force-limiting spring stack 54 is a zigzag spring line rising from the wedge 52 into the cavity.

An elongated lever, the latch handle 50, is pivoted to the latch housing 58 at a small circle at the upper right of the cavity. From that pivot a short arm reaches down and left onto the upper end of that stack, and the lever runs up and right out through a gap between the top wall and the right wall, leaning right past upright, the over-center position.

A slender pin, the indicator pin 56, rises from that stack through a hole in the top wall.
